title: Short Stuff: What's a mudlarker?
summary: Short Stuff episode explaining mudlarking, the hobby of searching the muddy foreshore of the River Thames in London at low tide for historic objects. Josh and Chuck cover its origins as a way for poor people to scrape a living in the 18th and 19th centuries, its modern status as a pastime, why the Thames is rich in finds (dense history, tidal action, and a river cleaned up after decades of dumping), and preservation in mud. They discuss the permit required from the Port of London Authority (about 35 pounds, roughly a month to get, digging limited to about three inches), protected archaeological zones like the Tower of London area, the Treasure Act and Portable Antiquities Scheme for reporting valuable finds, and common finds like clay pipes. Safety hazards include tides, slippery rocks, and rat-urine-borne Weil's disease. The episode closes with the story of the Doves Press typeface, whose metal matrices were thrown into the Thames, and designer Robert Green's later recovery of molds with help from the Port of London Authority dive team in 2014.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic of mudlarking and joke about whether the term means 'having a lark in the mud.'

segments.title: What mudlarking is and its history
segments.summary: Mudlarking is walking the Thames mudbanks at low tide to collect items to sell. In the 18th and 19th centuries poorer people made a living this way; today it is a hobby similar to beachcombing with metal detectors or magnet fishing.

segments.title: Why the Thames is cleaned up but rich in finds
segments.summary: The Thames was a dumping ground for many years and was heavily polluted until a cleanup about sixty years ago. Centuries of dense settlement left many objects in its mud.

segments.title: Tides and preservation of finds
segments.summary: Strong tides twice daily expose the riverbed and scour deposits onto the foreshore. Objects buried in mud survive in good condition, illustrated by a well-preserved shoe with impressions of the wearer's foot.

segments.title: Permits and digging limits
segments.summary: Digging on the Thames foreshore requires a permit from the Port of London Authority, which takes about a month and costs about 35 pounds, and allows digging only about three inches deep.

segments.title: Protected archaeological areas
segments.summary: Some Thames sites are off limits, such as areas near the Tower of London and the Roman and Saxon site of Queenhithe, which are protected cultural and archaeological sites.

segments.title: Treasure laws and reporting finds
segments.summary: Valuable finds must be reported to a finds liaison officer and recorded in the Portable Antiquities Scheme; museums may buy them and finders may be compensated. Worthless finds can be kept.

segments.title: Clay pipes as common finds
segments.summary: Clay pipes from the sixteenth century onward are very common finds because they were discarded like cigarette butts once used or clogged with tar.

segments.title: Safety hazards and Weil's disease
segments.summary: Hazards include being caught by the rising tide, slipping on algae-covered rocks, and infection risk; Weil's disease is spread through rat urine in the water. Gloves and boots are recommended.

segments.title: Doves Press typeface recovered from the Thames
segments.summary: Cobden-Sanderson, co-owner of the Doves Press with Emery Walker, threw the press's metal typeface matrices into the Thames after a dispute, leaving no other copies. Designer Robert Green later digitized the Doves Roman typeface from printed examples and recovered molds from the river.

segments.title: Port of London Authority dive team recovery
segments.summary: In 2014 Robert Green got the Port of London Authority dive team to retrieve the Doves type from the river, and the hosts praise the Doves Roman font.
topics: Port of London Authority dive team

segments.title: Outro and sponsor credit
segments.summary: Hosts recommend looking up more mudlarking finds, remind listeners to get a permit, and close with the show's production credit.
